I have been farming these 15 mu for 30 years, and at 53 I know every piece of this land. My husband and my child both work off-farm in town, so the daily work is mostly on my shoulders, though they come back for harvest and heavy jobs. That means I have to manage my labor carefully—I cannot afford to try fancy new methods or waste time on things that might fail.

Our 10 mu of wheat-maize rotation is the backbone of the farm. I will sow improved wheat seed in October after rotary tilling the soil. I put down compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea at jointing, because that is when the wheat is hungriest. I will irrigate three times using our well: before winter to protect the seedlings, at jointing, and during grain filling. I spray pesticides three times—herbicide early, then insecticide and fungicide when I see problems in the field. I expect about 480 kg per mu. As soon as the wheat is harvested in early June, I plant hybrid maize seed directly into the stubble without tilling. No-tillage saves precious days and labor, and the hybrid seed gives good yield. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing, irrigate twice if the rain is not enough—once when the plants are growing fast and once at flowering—and spray two or three times for weeds and pests. I hope for 550 kg per mu.

The remaining 5 mu I plant with cotton. Cotton gives a better price than grain but needs more attention. I will rotary till in spring and sow hybrid cotton seed in late April. Cotton needs plenty of potash, so I use compound fertilizer with good potassium and topdress during flowering. I irrigate three times—at budding, flowering, and boll formation—and spray four times for bollworms and aphids. I also do the pruning and topping myself. I expect around 280 kg of seed cotton per mu. I do not waste water because pumping from the well costs electricity; I only irrigate at the critical stages. After 30 years, I stick with what works—I buy good seed, fertilize properly, spray when needed, and do not take risks.
